deep.reconstruction:
Context (p.179): Gauss works on the sphere with R = right angle, ϱ = quadrant of a great circle, λ = one eighth of the sphere's area. F(a,b) is the area of a spherical quadrilateral with three right angles (a spherical Lambert quadrilateral). Call it OPQD with right angles at O, P, Q. The sides adjacent to the middle right angle at O are OP = a and OQ = b. The opposite sides are QD = α (opposite a) and PD = β (opposite b). The fourth angle at D is R+ω. For infinitesimal a he writes F(a,b) = a·f(b), and for infinitesimal b, f(b) = k·b.

This page derives f(b), and with it the area of the sphere, from area relations alone.

(1) ω = (R/λ)F(a,b). Area is proportional to spherical excess, and the octant (trirectangular triangle) has excess R and area λ (Girard).

(2) α = (ϱ/λ)F(a, ϱ−β) and (3) β = (ϱ/λ)F(b, ϱ−α). These come from the auxiliary figure of p.179. Extending the sides to quadrants produces a second trirectangular quadrilateral with sides a and ϱ−β, whose excess, in angle units, equals α. Modern check (unit sphere): the excess satisfies sin ω = sin a sin b, and the opposite side satisfies sin α = sin a cos β. Hence the excess of (a, π/2−β) is arcsin(sin a cos β) = α.

(4) F(a,ϱ) = aλ/ϱ. With b = ϱ the excess equals a, measured in the units R ↔ ϱ.

(5) f(ϱ) = λ/ϱ, which is (4) with a infinitesimal.

For infinitesimal a, (2) gives α = (ϱ/λ)·a·f(ϱ−β), which is infinitesimal. Then (3) gives β = (ϱ/λ)F(b,ϱ) + infinitesimal = b + infinitesimal, using (4) and the symmetry of F.

(6) The total differential is dF(a,b) = F(da,β) + F(db,α) = da·f(β) + db·f(α). Increasing a by da adds a thin trirectangular strip with sides da and β along PD; similarly for db along QD.

With only b varying: dF = db·f(α). For infinitesimal a: d(a f(b)) = db·f(α) = db·kα = db·(ϱ/λ)·a·k·f(ϱ−β). Putting β = b and dividing by the constant a:

(7) df(b)/db = (ϱk/λ)·f(ϱ−b).

Replacing b by ϱ−b gives df(ϱ−b)/db = −(ϱk/λ)·f(b). [The linear system is mine to name: write c = ϱk/λ.] Set B = f(ϱ−b) + i f(b) and B' = f(ϱ−b) − i f(b). Then dB = icB db and dB' = −icB' db, so B = C e^{icb} and B' = C' e^{−icb}.

Initial values: f(0) = 0 (since f(b) = kb for small b) and f(ϱ) = λ/ϱ by (5). So B(0) = B'(0) = λ/ϱ, giving C = C' = λ/ϱ.

On the next page this yields f(b) = (λ/ϱ) sin(cb) and f(ϱ−b) = (λ/ϱ) cos(cb). The condition f(ϱ) = λ/ϱ forces sin(ϱ²k/λ) = 1, hence ϱ²k/λ = π/2 and f(b) = (λ/ϱ) sin(πb/(2ϱ)).

[My interpretation:] k is the conversion factor between infinitesimal rectangle area k·a·b and the side units. So λ = 2kϱ²/π, and the full sphere has area 8λ = 16kϱ²/π. With ϱ = πr/2 and k = 1 this is 4πr². The page is thus an intrinsic, area-based derivation of the sine law F(a,b) ≈ a sin b and of the sphere's area, using no trigonometry. In spirit it matches Gauss's 'Sphärik' and non-Euclidean investigations.
errors: No substantive errors on this page.
Minor gap: sin(ϱ²k/λ) = 1 only gives ϱ²k/λ = π/2 + 2πn. Choosing n = 0 needs an extra argument, e.g. f > 0 on (0,ϱ) or f(b) ~ kb with f monotone. This choice is made on the next page.
Equation (2)/(3) relies on the auxiliary figure from p.179 without written proof. The relations are correct.
Setting β = b inside f(ϱ−β) uses the earlier remark that β differs only infinitesimally from b. This is legitimate to first order in a.

results.what: Area of a spherical trirectangular quadrilateral is proportional to its excess: ω = (R/λ)F(a,b)
results.modern_name: Girard's theorem (area = angular excess) applied to a Lambert quadrilateral

results.what: Complementary-quadrilateral relations α = (ϱ/λ)F(a, ϱ−β), β = (ϱ/λ)F(b, ϱ−α), F(a,ϱ) = aλ/ϱ
results.modern_name: Relations in spherical Lambert quadrilaterals (equivalent to sin α = sin a cos β, sin ω = sin a sin b)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical trigonometry (Lambert-quadrilateral formulas; Lambert 1766 for the quadrilateral)

results.what: Differential/functional equation f'(b) = (ϱk/λ) f(ϱ−b), solved via B = f(ϱ−b) ± i f(b) to get f(b) = (λ/ϱ) sin(πb/(2ϱ)), hence the area of the sphere, from area additivity alone
results.modern_name: Synthetic/analytic derivation of spherical trigonometric functions (and sphere area) from area of Lambert quadrilaterals; analogue of absolute-geometry derivations of trigonometry
results.usually_credited_to: Similar programs: J. Bolyai, Appendix (1832), §26 spherical trigonometry independent of the parallel axiom; Lobachevsky

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is classical and correct. What is notable is the method: an intrinsic derivation of the sine dependence of Lambert-quadrilateral area, and of the sphere's area, from area additivity via a complex-exponential solution of a functional differential equation. It fits Gauss's known 'Sphärik' and non-Euclidean interests, which are documented in letters and in Werke VIII, so it is a notable unpublished detail rather than a new attribution. The neighbouring Pentagramma mirificum is published (Werke III); whether this exact derivation is printed is unclear.

checkable.asserts: Unit sphere: the excess of the quadrilateral with sides (a, ϱ−β) equals α, where sin α = sin a cos β (eq. 2).
Eq. 6: dF/db = f(α) with F = excess = asin(sin a sin b), α = atan(tan a cos b), f = sin (unit sphere); should be 0 for 0<a,b<pi/2.
For infinitesimal a, F(a,b) = a f(b) with f(b) = sin b on the unit sphere.
f(b) = (λ/ϱ) sin(πb/(2ϱ)) with k = πλ/(2ϱ²) satisfies eq. 7: f'(b) = (ϱk/λ) f(ϱ−b).
B = (λ/ϱ) e^{icb} solves dB = icB db.
ϱ²k/λ = π/2 implies sphere area 8λ = 4πr² when ϱ = πr/2 and k = 1.

transcription_corrections: The symbol transcribed as 'ℓ' throughout (eqs. 2, 3, 6 and the text) is Gauss's β, the side opposite b; e.g. α = (ϱ/λ)F(a, ϱ−β), dF = da·f β + db·f α.
'oder da hier ℓ = b gesetzt werden [kann]' should read 'β = b gesetzt werden kann'.
Next page: 'f(ξ − b)' should be 'f(ϱ − b)'.
'd a f b' is d(a·f(b)) with a held constant.
